title: DiRotQ: Rotation-Aware Quantization for 4-bit Diffusion Transformers

paper.title: DiRotQ: Rotation-Aware Quantization for 4-bit Diffusion Transformers
paper.abstract: Abstract Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve state-of-the-art image generation quality but incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference. While aggressive Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) to 4-bit precision offers significant efficiency gains, it typically results in severe quality degradation. Existing approaches, including smoothing-based methods, mixed-precision schemes, rotation techniques, and low-rank residual methods, partially mitigate this issue but still leave a noticeable gap to FP16/BF16 performance. In this work, we introduce DiRotQ , a W4A4 PTQ framework that mitigates this degradation through rotation-aware activation quantization. DiRotQ identifies a low-rank subspace capturing dominant activation variance via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), preserving coefficients in this subspace at higher precision while quantizing the remaining components to 4-bit. Activations are rotated into the PCA basis at inference time using calibration-derived orthogonal transformations, while the inverse rotation is fused into the layer weights offline. Combined with GPTQ-based ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) weight quantization, DiRotQ achieves an FID ( ↓ ) (\downarrow) of 15.9 15.9 and PSNR ( ↑ ) (\uparrow) of 19.1 19.1 dB on PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) over the MJHQ-30K ( Li et al., 2024 ) dataset, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) (FID 18.9 18.9 , PSNR 17.6 17.6 ) under the same INT W4A4 setting. Beyond standard metrics, we introduce a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol for diffusion model quantization, the first such evaluation in this setting, providing a more holistic assessment of perceptual quality and prompt alignment under aggressive compression. On the systems side, we implement a Triton-based ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) custom kernel to enable efficient end-to-end inference, reducing memory usage of the 12B FLUX.1-dev model by 2.1 × 2.1\times and delivering 2.3 × 2.3\times speedup over the BF16 baseline, on a 24 GB RTX 4090 GPU. Our codebase is available here .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1 : PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) Block 2, self-attention input activation distributions across 20 20 denoising timesteps. (a) Temporal variance for channels 239 and 364. (b) Original activations show severe channel-wise variance with large outliers ( max / median = 83 × \nicefrac{{\max}}{{\text{median}}}=83\times ). (c, d) PCA isolates outliers in a 16 16 -bit subspace (red), reducing the ratio in the remaining 4 4 -bit channels (blue) to 16 × 16\times . (e, f) Rotation further equalizes the 4 4 -bit subspace ( green ), bringing the ratio down to 2 × 2\times . Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ) have become the dominant generative framework for visual, audio, and multimodal generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance in text-to-image ( Avrahami et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Balaji et al., 2022 ; Ye et al., 2023 ) , image synthesis ( Podell et al., 2023 ; Chang et al., 2022 ) , and audio generation ( Kong et al., 2020 ) . Despite their strong performance, diffusion models are computationally and memory intensive, requiring iterative denoising over many timesteps, with each step incurring additional cost from the quadratic complexity of self-attention over image patch tokens. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) reduces memory footprint and inference latency with minimal retraining cost ( Shang et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . As shown in prior work ( Li et al., 2025 ) , diffusion models remain compute-bound even at small batch sizes, making weight-only quantization insufficient for speedup. Both weights and activations must use the same precision; otherwise, weights are upcast during computation, negating any performance gains. While prior work has explored low-bit quantization, a gap to full-precision baselines persists under aggressive settings. In this work, we focus on jointly quantizing activations and weights to enable efficient low-bit inference while narrowing this gap. We propose DiRotQ , a PCA-based rotation-aware quantization framework that aligns the quantization basis with the activation distribution to enable accurate W4A4 inference. As shown in Figure 1 , raw DiT activations exhibit pronounced timestep-(Figure 1 a) and channel-dependent (Figure 1 b) outliers, making low-bit quantization highly error-prone. SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) addresses this by shifting activation outliers into the weights and applying low-rank decomposition; however, because it operates in weight space, SVDQuant only partially captures activation statistics. In contrast, DiRotQ operates directly in activation space, rotating activations into their PCA basis to concentrate outlier energy into a small high-variance subspace that is retained in high precision. The remaining components become significantly more uniform across channels and timesteps (max/median ≈ 16 × \approx 16\times vs. ≈ 83 × \approx 83\times ), and an additional orthogonal rotation further equalizes this residual subspace (max/median ≈ 2 × \approx 2\times ), enabling efficient 4-bit quantization (Figure 1 f). This improved conditioning translates into higher quantization fidelity: as shown in Figures 2 and 6 , DiRotQ substantially improves activation QSNR by 5 5 – 10 10 dB over SVDQuant and RTN across transformer blocks and denoising timesteps. Although rotation-based quantization has been highly effective for LLMs (e.g., QuaRot ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , ResQ ( Saxena et al., 2025 ) , SpinQuant ( Liu et al., 2025 ) ), prior work ( Li et al., 2025 ) argued it is inapplicable to diffusion models. First, due to adaptive normalization layers (e.g., AdaLN ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) ), rotation cannot be absorbed into preceding weights, requiring explicit handling during inference. Second, diffusion models exhibit strong timestep-dependent variation in activation magnitudes, making naive cross-layer sharing of rotation matrices ineffective. DiRotQ addresses both challenges with a tailored design: rotations are computed per layer to respect layer-specific statistics, and a single time-averaged PCA basis per layer is shared across timesteps, with timestep-dependent magnitude shifts absorbed by per-token activation scales and a small high-precision tail. This design keeps only the forward rotation online while fusing its inverse into the static weights, making rotation-based W4A4 quantization practical and effective for DiTs. We evaluate DiRotQ on three state-of-the-art DiT models, PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) , and SANA-1.6B ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , across two diverse datasets (MJHQ-30K ( Li et al., 2024 ) and sDCI ( Urbanek et al., 2024 ) ), reporting quality and similarity metrics. To better assess the impact of quantization on generation quality, we further adopt a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol , which has recently emerged as a reliable alternative for assessing text-to-image models ( Chen et al., 2024c ; Hayes et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . Unlike traditional methods, VLM-based judges jointly reason about visual quality and prompt alignment, making them well-suited for capturing subtle degradation introduced by low-bit quantization. To our knowledge, this is the first work to incorporate VLM-based evaluation for diffusion model quantization, enabling a more holistic assessment of generation quality under aggressive compression. We make the following contributions: 1. We propose DiRotQ, a W4A4 post-training quantization framework for DiTs that uses PCA-based activation rotation to decompose activations into a high-variance subspace retained in higher precision and a low-variance subspace quantized to 4-bit, substantially reducing quantization error. 2. We adopt a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol for diffusion model quantization to provide a more holistic assessment of perceptual quality and prompt alignment. 3. We implement a custom Triton-based kernel for efficient rotation and achieve runtime speedup and memory reduction on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with our quantized models.

sections.heading: Diffusion models
sections.text: Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) generate samples via iterative denoising and have achieved strong performance in text-to-image tasks ( Balaji et al., 2022 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ) . Early diffusion models primarily relied on UNet-based architectures ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) . More recent work has explored transformer-based designs, leading to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Bao et al., 2023 ) , which improve scalability and generation quality in models such as PixArt ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) , FLUX ( Labs, 2024 ) , and Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . Existing efforts have explored accelerating diffusion models through faster samplers ( Song et al., 2020 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2024b ) , and system-level optimizations, including efficient architectures ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023b ) , sparsification ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) , computation optimization via caching and token reduction methods ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Bolya et al., 2022 ) , and quantization ( Shang et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we focus on quantization, which provides an effective trade-off between compression and generation quality, reducing memory and latency with minimal degradation.

sections.heading: Quantization
sections.text: Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) reduces the precision of weights and activations to improve efficiency without retraining. In LLMs, methods such as GPTQ ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) and AWQ ( Lin et al., 2024 ) focus on weight quantization, while SmoothQuant ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) and LLM.int8() ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) target both activation and weight quantization and address activation outliers via scaling or mixed precision. Rotation-based approaches improve activation quantization by suppressing outliers through orthogonal transformations. QuaRot ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) applies fixed Hadamard rotations to enable end-to-end 4-bit quantization, while TurboQuant ( Zandieh et al., 2026 ) leverages random orthogonal rotations for KV cache quantization. ResQ ( Saxena et al., 2025 ) employs PCA-based rotations to decompose weights and activations into high- and low-variance subspaces, enabling mixed-precision quantization that preserves salient components and SpinQuant ( Liu et al., 2025 ) learns rotation matrices to reduce the gap to full precision. Despite their effectiveness in LLMs, these approaches do not directly extend to diffusion models, where the iterative denoising process introduces pronounced timestep-dependent variation in activation statistics. Unlike LLMs with relatively stable distributions, diffusion models exhibit large shifts across timesteps, making static quantization ineffective. Early works such as Q-Diffusion ( Li et al., 2023a ) and PTQ4DM ( Shang et al., 2023 ) address this via timestep-aware calibration, while PTQD ( He et al., 2023 ) accounts for error accumulation across denoising steps. In addition to timestep-dependent variation, the adoption of DiTs ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) introduces further challenges, including token-wise spatial variance, channel-wise outliers, and condition-wise variation from Classifier-Free Guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . Recent methods tackle these issues from different angles: PTQ4DiT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) and DiTAS ( Dong and Zhang, 2025 ) mitigate outliers via transformation and smoothing, ViDiT-Q ( Zhao et al., 2025b ) and DGQ ( Ryu et al., 2025 ) introduce fine-grained dynamic quantization, and Q-DiT ( Chen et al., 2025a ) adapts quantization granularity based on activation statistics. FP4DiT ( Chen et al., 2025b ) explores floating-point quantization (W4A6) on DiTs to better align with non-uniform weight/activation distributions and MSFP ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) pursues 4-bit FP quantization through timestep-aware LoRA fine-tuning. Rotation-based PTQ methods such as ConvRot ( Huang and others, 2025 ) and LRQ-DiT ( Yang et al., 2025 ) use Hadamard and log-rotation transforms to suppress activation outliers in DiTs under low-bit settings. More recently, SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) handles outliers by separating them into a high-precision low-rank branch while quantizing the residual to 4-bit precision, enabling end-to-end W4A4 inference. Despite these advances, a gap to full-precision performance remains under aggressive low-bit settings, as existing methods address individual challenges in isolation. For example, SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) at INT4, applied to PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , exhibits ∼ 14 % \sim 14\% higher FID score than the 16 16 -bit floating point baseline, even after nontrivial optimization. In this work, we propose a PCA-based approach that jointly captures timestep-, token-, and channel-wise variations for accurate and efficient 4-bit quantization.

sections.heading: 3 Quantization preliminaries
sections.text: Quantization is a model compression technique that reduces the numerical precision of tensor elements, typically from 32-bit or 16-bit floating-point (FP32, FP16, BF16) to lower-bit representations such as 8-bit (INT8, FP8), or even 4-bit (INT4, NVFP4, MXFP4) formats, enabling more efficient computation and storage. In contrast, activation quantization is more challenging, as discussed in Section 1 , and in this work we focus on mitigating it. Both 𝐔 \mathbf{U} and 𝐑 \mathbf{R} are fixed across timesteps . This design preserves high-variance components with minimal error while efficiently quantizing low-variance residuals, thereby reducing overall activation quantization error and maintaining model accuracy.

sections.heading: Models and Datasets
sections.text: We evaluate DiRotQ on three text-to-image DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) models: PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) , and SANA ( Xie et al., 2025 ) . PixArt- Σ \Sigma is a 600M-parameter DiT optimized for high-resolution generation, while FLUX.1-dev is a large 12B-parameter model, and SANA is a 1.6B-parameter model designed for improved scalability. We report results in each model’s native precision (FP16 for PixArt- Σ \Sigma , BF16 for FLUX.1-dev and SANA). Following prior work ( Li et al., 2023a ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , we use 128 prompts from the COCO Captions dataset ( Chen et al., 2015 ) for calibration. We evaluate generalization on two diverse prompt sets: MJHQ-30K ( Li et al., 2024 ) , which captures diverse artistic styles, and sDCI ( Urbanek et al., 2024 ) , which focuses on realistic and detailed captions. For both datasets, we randomly sample 5K prompts for evaluation. See Appendix D for details on models and datasets.

sections.heading: Baselines
sections.text: We compare DiRotQ with the following PTQ techniques: • PTQ4DiT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) enables W4A8 quantization for DiTs by addressing salient channel outliers and temporal activation variation via channel-wise calibration. However, we do not apply it to FLUX.1-dev due to its 12B parameter scale, where layer-wise AdaRound ( Nagel et al., 2020 ) calibration becomes prohibitively expensive (over 60 hours per run on an A100 GPU), making iterative tuning impractical. • Q-DiT ( Chen et al., 2025a ) addresses spatial and temporal variance in DiTs by combining automatic quantization granularity allocation across channels with sample-wise dynamic activation quantization across timesteps, improving robustness and accuracy under low-bit settings (e.g., W4A8). • ViDiT-Q ( Zhao et al., 2025b ) addresses activation outliers using per-token quantization and smoothing ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , combined with rotation-based transformations ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , achieving lossless W8A8 quantization on PixArt- Σ \Sigma and strong performance at lower bit-widths (e.g., W4A8). • SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) first shifts activation outliers to weights via smoothing ( Xiao et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) , then uses SVD-based ( Eckart and Young, 1936 ) low-rank decomposition to split tensors into a high-precision branch for outliers and a low-bit branch for residuals, enabling efficient W4A4 quantization of DiT models.

sections.heading: Metrics
sections.text: Following prior work ( Li et al., 2023a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate model performance using quality and similarity metrics. For quality, we report Fréchet Inception Distance ( FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , ↓ \downarrow ), which measures distributional distance between generated and real images, and Image Reward ( IR ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , ↑ \uparrow ) , which reflects alignment with human preferences. For similarity, we use Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity ( LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , ↓ \downarrow ) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio ( PSNR , ↑ \uparrow ), measuring perceptual and pixel-level fidelity, respectively. Since LPIPS and PSNR are computed against 16-bit reference outputs, they are undefined for reference rows (marked as – in tables). For holistic evaluation, we further employ a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol inspired by VIEScore ( Ku et al., 2024 ) , using a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) ( Yin et al., 2024a ) to assess Semantic Consistency (SC) and Perceptual Quality (PQ) on a 1 1 - 10 10 scale ( ↑ \uparrow ) . sections.heading: Implementation details
sections.text: Following SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) , we adopt per-token dynamic activation quantization and per-channel static weight quantization for 8 8 -bit settings. For 4 4 -bit INT, we apply per-group quantization to both activations and weights (group size 64 64 ) with 16 16 -bit scaling factors, using asymmetric activation quantization. For 4 4 -bit FP, we use NVFP4 NVIDIA Corporation (2024) , which supports group size 16 16 with FP8 scaling. For VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, since the original VIEScore backbone (GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) ) requires a commercial API, we instead employ Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and InternVL2-8B ( Chen et al., 2024d ) as open-source alternatives, approximating the VIEScore protocol by: (i) prompting each model to produce a step-by-step rationale prior to assigning numeric scores ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) , (ii) using low-temperature sampling to reduce score variance, and (iii) computing the overall score as a geometric mean of SC and PQ. Appendix F provides full details of the quantization scheme and VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol, including scoring scheme and judge prompts.

sections.heading: Visual quality results
sections.text: We present quantitative results in Table 1 across multiple models and precision settings, along with visual qualitative comparisons in Figure 3 . We exclude PTQ4DiT from the qualitative comparisons in the interest of space, as it consistently underperforms relative to the other methods. Figure 3 illustrates visual comparisons across three models on the MJHQ-30K dataset. We observe that DiRotQ at 4 4 -bit precision consistently outperforms other methods, even surpassing the W4A8 technique, achieving closer similarity to the 16 16 -bit models. Table 1 indicates that DiRotQ consistently outperforms prior PTQ methods across all models and datasets, with the most significant gains at W4A4 precision. On PixArt- Σ \Sigma , DiRotQ INT W4A4 achieves FID 15.9 15.9 and IR 0.941 0.941 on MJHQ-30K, substantially improving over SVDQuant (FID 18.9 18.9 , IR 0.871 0.871 ), while also delivering higher fidelity (PSNR 19.1 19.1 vs. 17.6 17.6 ) and lower perceptual error (LPIPS 0.236 0.236 vs. 0.319 0.319 ). These improvements extend to sDCI and NVFP4 formats, where DiRotQ consistently reduces LPIPS and improves PSNR, indicating better preservation of visual details. For larger models such as FLUX.1-dev and SANA-1.6B, DiRotQ maintains comparable or better FID while significantly improving similarity metrics, highlighting stronger reconstruction quality under aggressive quantization. Notably, DiRotQ at W4A4 substantially closes the gap to BF16 (e.g., FLUX.1-dev on MJHQ-30K, IR 0.934 vs. 0.939), demonstrating that PCA-based rotation effectively mitigates activation quantization error and enables high-quality 4-bit inference across diverse DiT architectures. Additional quantitative metrics, including CLIP Score, CLIP IQA, and SSIM, and visual qualitative comparisons are provided in Appendix G.1 (Table 3 , Figures 9 , 10 , and 11 ).

sections.heading: Memory saving and speedup
sections.text: Figure 4 shows the memory savings and inference speedup of DiRotQ on FLUX.1-dev. Following SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate the memory savings and end-to-end speedup of DiRotQ on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 desktop GPU ( NVIDIA Corporation, 2022 ) . For efficient 4 4 -bit INT matrix multiplication, we use the optimized kernel provided by the Nunchaku inference engine ( Li et al., 2025 ) . For the rotation operations, we implement an efficient Triton ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) kernel. Compared to the BF16 baseline, DiRotQ achieves an overall 2.1 × 2.1\times reduction in DiT inference memory, after accounting for overhead from high-precision branches, rotation matrices, and unquantized normalization layers. The memory savings mainly come from quantizing the weights of the linear layers, as activation memory accounts for only about 2 % 2\% of the weight memory. As a result, DiRotQ has nearly the same memory footprint as the INT4 weight-only quantization variant (Figure 4 a). For latency, when the batch size is 1 1 and the BF16 model fits on GPU, DiRotQ achieves a 2.3 × 2.3\times end-to-end speedup per denoising timestep compared to BF16. In contrast, the INT4 weight-only baseline provides little to no speedup, since it does not enable low-precision compute and introduces additional overhead from upcasting weights to BF16 (Figure 4 b). When increasing the batch size to 2 2 , the BF16 model no longer fits entirely in GPU memory and requires per-layer CPU offloading, while DiRotQ still fits entirely in GPU memory. This avoids offloading overhead and results in a 9.2 × 9.2\times speedup over BF16 (Figure 4 d). Figure 4 : Memory usage and one-step latency for FLUX.1-dev across batch sizes 1 and 2. DiRotQ (INT W4A4) reduces memory by 2.1 × 2.1\times and achieves 2.3 × 2.3\times speedup at batch size 1 and 9.2 × 9.2\times at batch size 2 over BF16; the larger gain at batch size 2 is driven by eliminating CPU offloading.

sections.heading: Component ablation.
sections.text: Table 2 shows the contribution of each DiRotQ component on PixArt- Σ \Sigma over MJHQ-30K. Naive INT W4A4 RTN quantization degrades FID severely from 16.6 16.6 (FP16) to 40.3 40.3 , confirming that 4 4 -bit quantization is highly error-prone without outlier mitigation. Adding PCA-based rotation reduces FID to 19.7 19.7 by isolating outlier energy into a high-precision subspace, while the residual orthogonal rotation provides further consistent gains across all metrics. GPTQ on the weight residual has a synergistic effect with the rotations, bringing DiRotQ to FID 15.9 15.9 and PSNR 19.1 19.1 and matching FP16 quality. The same trend holds for NVFP4.

sections.heading: High-precision tail fraction.
sections.text: For PixArt- Σ \Sigma on MJHQ-30K, we sweep the FP16 tail fraction r r from 5 % 5\% to 25 % 25\% for different layers, and across various timesteps, and find that activation QSNR improves sharply up to r = 10 % r{=}10\% and saturates beyond, with gains under 0.5 0.5 dB per additional 5 % 5\% . This reflects PCA’s ability to concentrate outlier variance into a few leading components. We therefore use r = 10 % r{=}10\% throughout the paper, balancing quality and overhead (Section 5.2 ); full results are in Appendix G.3 .

sections.heading: 6 Limitations and broader impacts
sections.text: DiRotQ improves the efficiency of DiTs by reducing memory and compute costs via 4-bit PTQ, enabling efficient deployment of large-scale generative models in resource-constrained settings. While we focus on text-to-image generation, extending DiRotQ to video remains an important direction, though temporal dependencies across frames introduce additional challenges not addressed here. Qur PCA basis is also shared across timesteps to enable offline weight fusion; exploring per-timestep-group rotations under tighter memory budgets is left to future work. More broadly, although our method supports wider adoption of generative models, it does not mitigate risks of misuse such as generating harmful or misleading content. Addressing these concerns requires complementary safeguards, responsible deployment, and further research into trustworthy generative systems.

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: In this work, we introduce DiRotQ, a rotation-aware 4-bit PTQ framework specifically designed for diffusion transformers. By leveraging PCA-based transformations to better align activation statistics, DiRotQ effectively mitigates quantization errors arising from timestep-dependent variation and activation outliers. To provide a comprehensive assessment of generative performance, we further integrate a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol, offering a holistic view of perceptual quality and prompt alignment. Our implementation includes an efficient Triton-based rotation kernel within the inference pipeline, significantly reducing memory footprint while improving runtime performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiRotQ consistently preserves high generation quality across diverse benchmarks. Notably, under the stringent W4A4 setting, DiRotQ achieves a PSNR of 24.6 on the MJHQ-30K dataset using the FLUX.1-dev architecture. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical scalability of our approach by reducing the memory usage of the 12B FLUX.1-dev model by 2.1 × 2.1\times and achieving a 2.3 × 2.3\times speedup over the BF16 baseline on a consumer-grade RTX 4090 GPU. These results highlight DiRotQ’s ability to narrow the gap to full-precision performance while enabling efficient deployment of large-scale diffusion models on resource-constrained hardware.

sections.heading: Models
sections.text: PixArt- Σ \Sigma [ 8 ] is a compact DiT (600M parameters) optimized for high-resolution (up to 4K) generation. It employs stacked transformer blocks with self-attention, cross-attention, and feed-forward layers, along with a key - value token compression mechanism to improve efficiency. FLUX.1-dev [ 33 ] is a guidance-distilled variant comprising 19 joint attention blocks [ 19 ] and 38 parallel attention blocks [ 15 ] , totaling 12B parameters. SANA [ 75 ] is a 1.6B-parameter DiT that reduces token complexity via a 32 × 32\times compressed latent space and replaces softmax attention with linear attention for improved scalability. Licenses for all models are listed in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Image generation settings
sections.text: For all models, we generate images at a resolution of 1024 × 1024 1024\times 1024 and use the hash_str_to_int utility from Lhotse [ 35 ] to derive deterministic per-prompt seeds for reproducibility. We employ the following model-specific generation settings: • PixArt- Σ \Sigma [ 8 ] . We apply Classifier-Free Guidance (CFG) [ 28 ] with a guidance scale of 4.5 4.5 , balancing image fidelity and text alignment by strengthening the conditional signal relative to the unconditional branch [ 28 ] , and run 20 20 inference steps. • FLUX.1-dev [ 33 ] . We use a CFG scale of 3.5 3.5 and perform all generations with 25 25 sampling steps using the FluxPipeline from the Hugging Face Diffusers library [ 68 ] . We evaluate on the dev variant, which employs single-branch guidance (i.e., not dual-branch CFG), with a maximum sequence length of 512 512 . • SANA [ 75 ] . We use 20 20 sampling steps with a CFG scale of 4.5 4.5 . Sampling is performed using the Flow-DPM scheduler [ 43 ] , which enables efficient and stable diffusion sampling.

sections.heading: Datasets
sections.text: MJHQ-30K [ 36 ] contains 30K prompts sourced from Midjourney [ 47 ] , spanning 10 categories (3K samples each) with diverse artistic styles. DCI [ 67 ] contains approximately 8K images with densely annotated captions, often spanning thousands of words; we use its summarized variant (sDCI), where captions are reduced to 77 tokens using large language models to align with diffusion model input constraints. The corresponding licenses for all datasets are provided in Appendix H .

sections.heading: Appendix E Additional evaluation metrics
sections.text: We provide three additional evaluation metrics to further assess semantic alignment and perceptual image quality: • CLIP Score [ 25 ] . Measures semantic alignment between a generated image and its text prompt using cosine similarity in the CLIP [ 54 ] embedding space. Higher scores indicate better text-image alignment. • CLIP IQA [ 69 ] . Evaluates perceptual image quality using CLIP [ 54 ] by comparing images against quality-related textual prompts. It captures artifacts such as blur and noise, with higher scores indicating better visual quality. • SSIM [ 72 ] . Measures structural similarity between images by comparing luminance, contrast, and structure. Higher values indicate greater similarity.

sections.heading: F.1 Quantization details
sections.text: Following SVDQuant [ 37 ] , we quantize both weights and activations of all linear layers to 4 4 -bit precision, except for the key and value projections in cross-attention, as they account for less than 5 % 5\% of total runtime. Additionally, input activations to adaptive normalization layers in the FLUX.1-dev model, and the down-projection layers in PixArt- Σ \Sigma , are kept in higher precision (W4A16). Across all layers, we identify the top 8 8 – 12 % 12\% high-variance activation components via PCA and retain them in high precision, while quantizing the remaining 88 88 – 92 % 92\% as residuals. The residual weights are quantized using GPTQ [ 20 ] , for which we use a damping factor of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 , following the original work, and a block size of 128 128 ; the former stabilizes the Hessian inversion, while the latter controls the granularity of column-wise quantization, balancing accuracy and efficiency. To compute the PCA projection matrices and perform GPTQ calibration, we use 128 128 randomly selected samples from COCO Captions [ 12 ] . Similarly, we have used a damping factor of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 for stability of PCA computation. The entire pipeline, including PCA and quantization, is executed on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU.

sections.heading: F.2 VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation details
sections.text: Standard metrics (e.g., FID, LPIPS, CLIP Score) capture only isolated aspects of image quality and fail to jointly reflect visual coherence and prompt fidelity, particularly under quantization where degradations may appear as subtle artifacts or semantic drift. To address this, VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation has gained traction as a more holistic alternative [ 13 , 22 ] , with recent work showing that multimodal language models provide reliable, fine-grained assessments aligned with human judgments [ 7 , 34 ] . In this work, we adopt a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol inspired by VIEScore [ 32 ] , which uses MLLMs as instruction-guided evaluators for conditional image generation. VIEScore reports that GPT-4o [ 51 ] judgments achieve a Spearman correlation of ρ = 0.4 \rho=0.4 with human judgments, approaching human-to-human agreement of ρ = 0.45 \rho=0.45 [ 83 ] . It evaluates images along two complementary axes: Semantic Consistency (SC), measuring prompt faithfulness, and Perceptual Quality (PQ), assessing visual coherence, sharpness, and artifacts, with the overall score computed as their geometric mean. Since GPT-4o requires a commercial API, we follow this two-axis structure using two open-source models, Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct [ 71 ] and InternVL2-8B [ 14 ] as judges, and report results from both models. Qwen2-VL provides holistic image-level assessment, while InternVL2’s dynamic tiling enables fine-grained local inspection, offering complementary coverage of global and local generation quality.

sections.heading: Evaluation setup
sections.text: For each method (DiRotQ and SVDQuant) and quantization format (INT4 and NVFP4), we evaluate 5K images generated by PixArt- Σ \Sigma on MJHQ-30K, spanning all 10 prompt categories. Each image is scored three times with low-temperature sampling ( do_sample=True , temperature=0.3 ), and the numeric scores are averaged across runs to reduce stochastic variance. Each image is scored via an independent API call using the pointwise prompt in Paragraph F.2 . As the judge evaluates one image at a time and never sees outputs from other methods in the same context, position bias across methods does not arise. Following VIEScore, the judge produces a step-by-step rationale before assigning scores [ 88 ] , improving alignment with human judgments. The enforced overall score is computed as Overall = SC × PQ \text{Overall}{=}\sqrt{\text{SC}\times\text{PQ}} , ensuring that failure on either dimension cannot be masked by the other. Differences below 0.01 0.01 are treated as ties.

sections.heading: Judge prompt
sections.text: The judge receives the text prompt and the generated image. The prompt instructs the model to return a JSON object with the rationale key first (think step-by-step before scoring), followed by Semantic_Consistency , Perceptual_Quality , and Overall on a 1–10 scale, with rubric anchors at every even level. The overall score is explicitly instructed to weight both dimensions equally and to penalize egregious failures in either dimension disproportionately. A text-to-image model generated this image from the prompt: {prompt} Evaluate this image and return ONLY a JSON object with "rationale" key FIRST (reason step-by-step before scoring), then: {"rationale": "<describe what you see, prompt alignment, artifacts>", "semantic_consistency": <1-10>, "perceptual_quality": <1-10>, "overall": <1-10>} SC: 10=all details match, 8=minor omissions, 6=key details wrong, 4=loosely related, 2=no relation, 1=incomprehensible. PQ: 10=photorealistic/no artifacts, 8=minor artifacts, 6=noticeable distortion, 4=significant artifacts, 2=severe, 1=broken. Overall: weight both terms equally by taking their geometric mean. sections.text: Table 3 reports additional perceptual and semantic metrics, including CLIP Score, CLIP IQA, and SSIM. On the sDCI dataset, DiRotQ shows consistent improvements in SSIM and maintains competitive CLIP IQA and CLIP Score across models, further confirming its effectiveness under 4 4 -bit quantization. sections.heading: G.3 High-precision tail fraction ablation
sections.text: A central design choice in DiRotQ is the rank ratio r r , which controls the fraction of PCA-rotated activation channels kept in FP16, while the remaining 1 − r 1-r are quantized to 4-bit. Increasing r r improves fidelity but also increases the memory footprint of the FP16 branch and the cost of online rotation, making it important to understand how performance scales with r r . We sweep r r from 5 % 5\% to 25 % 25\% and report activation QSNR, averaged over 28 transformer blocks of PixArt- Σ \Sigma on MJHQ-30K, for FFN Up, Self-attention QKV, and Cross-attention Q layers. Results across five denoising timesteps are shown in Figure 7 , with RTN as a reference baseline. Even with only a 5 % 5\% FP16 tail, DiRotQ already surpasses RTN by 10 10 – 20 20 dB across all layer types and timesteps, demonstrating that the PCA rotation itself, rather than the size of the high-precision tail, drives most of the quality improvement. Increasing r r to 10 % 10\% yields a further 2 2 – 3 3 dB gain, while larger values provide diminishing returns ( < 0.5 <0.5 dB per additional 5 % 5\% in most cases). This saturation arises because PCA concentrates most outlier variance into a small set of principal components, so even a modest FP16 tail captures the dominant quantization error. The trend is consistent across layers and timesteps, suggesting r = 10 % r=10\% as a robust default that avoids per-layer tuning while recovering most of the gap to the full-precision baseline. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 arXiv:2605.16732v1 [cs.CV] 16 May 2026 DiRotQ: Rotation-Aware Quantization for 4-bit Diffusion Transformers Sayeh Sharify Affiliation: d-Matrix Affiliation: Santa Clara, CA 95054 Email: sayehs@d-matrix.ai Mahsa Salmani Affiliation: d-Matrix Affiliation: Santa Clara, CA 95054 Email: msalmani@d-matrix.ai Hesham Mostafa Affiliation: d-Matrix Affiliation: Santa Clara, CA 95054 Email: hmostafa@d-matrix.ai Abstract Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) achieve state-of-the-art image generation quality but incur substantial memory and computational costs at inference. While aggressive Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) to 4-bit precision offers significant efficiency gains, it typically results in severe quality degradation. Existing approaches, including smoothing-based methods, mixed-precision schemes, rotation techniques, and low-rank residual methods, partially mitigate this issue but still leave a noticeable gap to FP16/BF16 performance. In this work, we introduce DiRotQ , a W4A4 PTQ framework that mitigates this degradation through rotation-aware activation quantization. DiRotQ identifies a low-rank subspace capturing dominant activation variance via Principal Component Analysis (PCA), preserving coefficients in this subspace at higher precision while quantizing the remaining components to 4-bit. Activations are rotated into the PCA basis at inference time using calibration-derived orthogonal transformations, while the inverse rotation is fused into the layer weights offline. Combined with GPTQ-based ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) weight quantization, DiRotQ achieves an FID ( ↓ ) (\downarrow) of 15.9 15.9 and PSNR ( ↑ ) (\uparrow) of 19.1 19.1 dB on PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) over the MJHQ-30K ( Li et al., 2024 ) dataset, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) (FID 18.9 18.9 , PSNR 17.6 17.6 ) under the same INT W4A4 setting. Beyond standard metrics, we introduce a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol for diffusion model quantization, the first such evaluation in this setting, providing a more holistic assessment of perceptual quality and prompt alignment under aggressive compression. On the systems side, we implement a Triton-based ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) custom kernel to enable efficient end-to-end inference, reducing memory usage of the 12B FLUX.1-dev model by 2.1 × 2.1\times and delivering 2.3 × 2.3\times speedup over the BF16 baseline, on a 24 GB RTX 4090 GPU. Our codebase is available here . 1 Introduction Figure 1 : PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) Block 2, self-attention input activation distributions across 20 20 denoising timesteps. (a) Temporal variance for channels 239 and 364. (b) Original activations show severe channel-wise variance with large outliers ( max / median = 83 × \nicefrac{{\max}}{{\text{median}}}=83\times ). (c, d) PCA isolates outliers in a 16 16 -bit subspace (red), reducing the ratio in the remaining 4 4 -bit channels (blue) to 16 × 16\times . (e, f) Rotation further equalizes the 4 4 -bit subspace ( green ), bringing the ratio down to 2 × 2\times . Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ) have become the dominant generative framework for visual, audio, and multimodal generation, achieving state-of-the-art performance in text-to-image ( Avrahami et al., 2022 ; Saharia et al., 2022 ; Balaji et al., 2022 ; Ye et al., 2023 ) , image synthesis ( Podell et al., 2023 ; Chang et al., 2022 ) , and audio generation ( Kong et al., 2020 ) . Despite their strong performance, diffusion models are computationally and memory intensive, requiring iterative denoising over many timesteps, with each step incurring additional cost from the quadratic complexity of self-attention over image patch tokens. Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) reduces memory footprint and inference latency with minimal retraining cost ( Shang et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . As shown in prior work ( Li et al., 2025 ) , diffusion models remain compute-bound even at small batch sizes, making weight-only quantization insufficient for speedup. Both weights and activations must use the same precision; otherwise, weights are upcast during computation, negating any performance gains. While prior work has explored low-bit quantization, a gap to full-precision baselines persists under aggressive settings. In this work, we focus on jointly quantizing activations and weights to enable efficient low-bit inference while narrowing this gap. We propose DiRotQ , a PCA-based rotation-aware quantization framework that aligns the quantization basis with the activation distribution to enable accurate W4A4 inference. As shown in Figure 1 , raw DiT activations exhibit pronounced timestep-(Figure 1 a) and channel-dependent (Figure 1 b) outliers, making low-bit quantization highly error-prone. SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) addresses this by shifting activation outliers into the weights and applying low-rank decomposition; however, because it operates in weight space, SVDQuant only partially captures activation statistics. In contrast, DiRotQ operates directly in activation space, rotating activations into their PCA basis to concentrate outlier energy into a small high-variance subspace that is retained in high precision. The remaining components become significantly more uniform across channels and timesteps (max/median ≈ 16 × \approx 16\times vs. ≈ 83 × \approx 83\times ), and an additional orthogonal rotation further equalizes this residual subspace (max/median ≈ 2 × \approx 2\times ), enabling efficient 4-bit quantization (Figure 1 f). This improved conditioning translates into higher quantization fidelity: as shown in Figures 2 and 6 , DiRotQ substantially improves activation QSNR by 5 5 – 10 10 dB over SVDQuant and RTN across transformer blocks and denoising timesteps. Although rotation-based quantization has been highly effective for LLMs (e.g., QuaRot ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , ResQ ( Saxena et al., 2025 ) , SpinQuant ( Liu et al., 2025 ) ), prior work ( Li et al., 2025 ) argued it is inapplicable to diffusion models. First, due to adaptive normalization layers (e.g., AdaLN ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) ), rotation cannot be absorbed into preceding weights, requiring explicit handling during inference. Second, diffusion models exhibit strong timestep-dependent variation in activation magnitudes, making naive cross-layer sharing of rotation matrices ineffective. DiRotQ addresses both challenges with a tailored design: rotations are computed per layer to respect layer-specific statistics, and a single time-averaged PCA basis per layer is shared across timesteps, with timestep-dependent magnitude shifts absorbed by per-token activation scales and a small high-precision tail. This design keeps only the forward rotation online while fusing its inverse into the static weights, making rotation-based W4A4 quantization practical and effective for DiTs. We evaluate DiRotQ on three state-of-the-art DiT models, PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) , and SANA-1.6B ( Xie et al., 2025 ) , across two diverse datasets (MJHQ-30K ( Li et al., 2024 ) and sDCI ( Urbanek et al., 2024 ) ), reporting quality and similarity metrics. To better assess the impact of quantization on generation quality, we further adopt a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol , which has recently emerged as a reliable alternative for assessing text-to-image models ( Chen et al., 2024c ; Hayes et al., 2025 ; Chen et al., 2024a ; Lee et al., 2024 ) . Unlike traditional methods, VLM-based judges jointly reason about visual quality and prompt alignment, making them well-suited for capturing subtle degradation introduced by low-bit quantization. To our knowledge, this is the first work to incorporate VLM-based evaluation for diffusion model quantization, enabling a more holistic assessment of generation quality under aggressive compression. We make the following contributions: 1. We propose DiRotQ, a W4A4 post-training quantization framework for DiTs that uses PCA-based activation rotation to decompose activations into a high-variance subspace retained in higher precision and a low-variance subspace quantized to 4-bit, substantially reducing quantization error. 2. We adopt a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol for diffusion model quantization to provide a more holistic assessment of perceptual quality and prompt alignment. 3. We implement a custom Triton-based kernel for efficient rotation and achieve runtime speedup and memory reduction on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU with our quantized models. 2 Related work Figure 2 : Per-block activation QSNR for the self-attention output projection across 28 28 PixArt- Σ \Sigma transformer blocks at five timesteps. DiRotQ outperforms RTN and SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) by 5 5 – 10 10 dB consistently across blocks and timesteps. Diffusion models Diffusion models ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) generate samples via iterative denoising and have achieved strong performance in text-to-image tasks ( Balaji et al., 2022 ; Rombach et al., 2022 ; Podell et al., 2023 ) . Early diffusion models primarily relied on UNet-based architectures ( Ronneberger et al., 2015 ) . More recent work has explored transformer-based designs, leading to Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ; Bao et al., 2023 ) , which improve scalability and generation quality in models such as PixArt ( Chen et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2024b ) , FLUX ( Labs, 2024 ) , and Stable Diffusion 3 ( Esser et al., 2024 ) . Existing efforts have explored accelerating diffusion models through faster samplers ( Song et al., 2020 ; Lu et al., 2022 ; Lu et al., 2025 ) , distillation ( Salimans and Ho, 2022 ; Song and Dhariwal, 2023 ; Luo et al., 2023 ; Sauer et al., 2024 ; Yin et al., 2024b ) , and system-level optimizations, including efficient architectures ( Kim et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2023b ) , sparsification ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Yuan et al., 2024 ) , computation optimization via caching and token reduction methods ( Ma et al., 2024 ; Bolya et al., 2022 ) , and quantization ( Shang et al., 2023 ; He et al., 2023 ; Li et al., 2025 ) . In this work, we focus on quantization, which provides an effective trade-off between compression and generation quality, reducing memory and latency with minimal degradation. Quantization Post-Training Quantization (PTQ) reduces the precision of weights and activations to improve efficiency without retraining. In LLMs, methods such as GPTQ ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) and AWQ ( Lin et al., 2024 ) focus on weight quantization, while SmoothQuant ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) and LLM.int8() ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) target both activation and weight quantization and address activation outliers via scaling or mixed precision. Rotation-based approaches improve activation quantization by suppressing outliers through orthogonal transformations. QuaRot ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) applies fixed Hadamard rotations to enable end-to-end 4-bit quantization, while TurboQuant ( Zandieh et al., 2026 ) leverages random orthogonal rotations for KV cache quantization. ResQ ( Saxena et al., 2025 ) employs PCA-based rotations to decompose weights and activations into high- and low-variance subspaces, enabling mixed-precision quantization that preserves salient components and SpinQuant ( Liu et al., 2025 ) learns rotation matrices to reduce the gap to full precision. Despite their effectiveness in LLMs, these approaches do not directly extend to diffusion models, where the iterative denoising process introduces pronounced timestep-dependent variation in activation statistics. Unlike LLMs with relatively stable distributions, diffusion models exhibit large shifts across timesteps, making static quantization ineffective. Early works such as Q-Diffusion ( Li et al., 2023a ) and PTQ4DM ( Shang et al., 2023 ) address this via timestep-aware calibration, while PTQD ( He et al., 2023 ) accounts for error accumulation across denoising steps. In addition to timestep-dependent variation, the adoption of DiTs ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) introduces further challenges, including token-wise spatial variance, channel-wise outliers, and condition-wise variation from Classifier-Free Guidance ( Ho and Salimans, 2022 ) . Recent methods tackle these issues from different angles: PTQ4DiT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) and DiTAS ( Dong and Zhang, 2025 ) mitigate outliers via transformation and smoothing, ViDiT-Q ( Zhao et al., 2025b ) and DGQ ( Ryu et al., 2025 ) introduce fine-grained dynamic quantization, and Q-DiT ( Chen et al., 2025a ) adapts quantization granularity based on activation statistics. FP4DiT ( Chen et al., 2025b ) explores floating-point quantization (W4A6) on DiTs to better align with non-uniform weight/activation distributions and MSFP ( Zhao et al., 2025a ) pursues 4-bit FP quantization through timestep-aware LoRA fine-tuning. Rotation-based PTQ methods such as ConvRot ( Huang and others, 2025 ) and LRQ-DiT ( Yang et al., 2025 ) use Hadamard and log-rotation transforms to suppress activation outliers in DiTs under low-bit settings. More recently, SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) handles outliers by separating them into a high-precision low-rank branch while quantizing the residual to 4-bit precision, enabling end-to-end W4A4 inference. Despite these advances, a gap to full-precision performance remains under aggressive low-bit settings, as existing methods address individual challenges in isolation. For example, SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) at INT4, applied to PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , exhibits ∼ 14 % \sim 14\% higher FID score than the 16 16 -bit floating point baseline, even after nontrivial optimization. In this work, we propose a PCA-based approach that jointly captures timestep-, token-, and channel-wise variations for accurate and efficient 4-bit quantization. 3 Quantization preliminaries Quantization is a model compression technique that reduces the numerical precision of tensor elements, typically from 32-bit or 16-bit floating-point (FP32, FP16, BF16) to lower-bit representations such as 8-bit (INT8, FP8), or even 4-bit (INT4, NVFP4, MXFP4) formats, enabling more efficient computation and storage. DiRotQ consistently outperforms prior techniques, surpasses the W4A8 method, and produces results closest to the 16 16 -bit baselines. 5.1 Setup Models and Datasets We evaluate DiRotQ on three text-to-image DiT ( Peebles and Xie, 2023 ) models: PixArt- Σ \Sigma ( Chen et al., 2024b ) , FLUX.1-dev ( Labs, 2024 ) , and SANA ( Xie et al., 2025 ) . PixArt- Σ \Sigma is a 600M-parameter DiT optimized for high-resolution generation, while FLUX.1-dev is a large 12B-parameter model, and SANA is a 1.6B-parameter model designed for improved scalability. We report results in each model’s native precision (FP16 for PixArt- Σ \Sigma , BF16 for FLUX.1-dev and SANA). Following prior work ( Li et al., 2023a ; Zhao et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , we use 128 prompts from the COCO Captions dataset ( Chen et al., 2015 ) for calibration. We evaluate generalization on two diverse prompt sets: MJHQ-30K ( Li et al., 2024 ) , which captures diverse artistic styles, and sDCI ( Urbanek et al., 2024 ) , which focuses on realistic and detailed captions. For both datasets, we randomly sample 5K prompts for evaluation. See Appendix D for details on models and datasets. Baselines We compare DiRotQ with the following PTQ techniques: • PTQ4DiT ( Wu et al., 2024 ) enables W4A8 quantization for DiTs by addressing salient channel outliers and temporal activation variation via channel-wise calibration. However, we do not apply it to FLUX.1-dev due to its 12B parameter scale, where layer-wise AdaRound ( Nagel et al., 2020 ) calibration becomes prohibitively expensive (over 60 hours per run on an A100 GPU), making iterative tuning impractical. • Q-DiT ( Chen et al., 2025a ) addresses spatial and temporal variance in DiTs by combining automatic quantization granularity allocation across channels with sample-wise dynamic activation quantization across timesteps, improving robustness and accuracy under low-bit settings (e.g., W4A8). • ViDiT-Q ( Zhao et al., 2025b ) addresses activation outliers using per-token quantization and smoothing ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , combined with rotation-based transformations ( Ashkboos et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2025 ) , achieving lossless W8A8 quantization on PixArt- Σ \Sigma and strong performance at lower bit-widths (e.g., W4A8). • SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) first shifts activation outliers to weights via smoothing ( Xiao et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) , then uses SVD-based ( Eckart and Young, 1936 ) low-rank decomposition to split tensors into a high-precision branch for outliers and a low-bit branch for residuals, enabling efficient W4A4 quantization of DiT models. Metrics Following prior work ( Li et al., 2023a ; Li et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate model performance using quality and similarity metrics. For quality, we report Fréchet Inception Distance ( FID ( Heusel et al., 2017 ) , ↓ \downarrow ), which measures distributional distance between generated and real images, and Image Reward ( IR ( Xu et al., 2023 ) , ↑ \uparrow ) , which reflects alignment with human preferences. For similarity, we use Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity ( LPIPS ( Zhang et al., 2018 ) , ↓ \downarrow ) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio ( PSNR , ↑ \uparrow ), measuring perceptual and pixel-level fidelity, respectively. Since LPIPS and PSNR are computed against 16-bit reference outputs, they are undefined for reference rows (marked as – in tables). For holistic evaluation, we further employ a VLM-as-a-Judge protocol inspired by VIEScore ( Ku et al., 2024 ) , using a Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM) ( Yin et al., 2024a ) to assess Semantic Consistency (SC) and Perceptual Quality (PQ) on a 1 1 - 10 10 scale ( ↑ \uparrow ) . For 4 4 -bit INT, we apply per-group quantization to both activations and weights (group size 64 64 ) with 16 16 -bit scaling factors, using asymmetric activation quantization. For 4 4 -bit FP, we use NVFP4 NVIDIA Corporation (2024) , which supports group size 16 16 with FP8 scaling. For VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation, since the original VIEScore backbone (GPT-4o ( OpenAI, 2024 ) ) requires a commercial API, we instead employ Qwen2-VL-7B-Instruct ( Wang et al., 2024 ) and InternVL2-8B ( Chen et al., 2024d ) as open-source alternatives, approximating the VIEScore protocol by: (i) prompting each model to produce a step-by-step rationale prior to assigning numeric scores ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) , (ii) using low-temperature sampling to reduce score variance, and (iii) computing the overall score as a geometric mean of SC and PQ. Memory saving and speedup Figure 4 shows the memory savings and inference speedup of DiRotQ on FLUX.1-dev. Following SVDQuant ( Li et al., 2025 ) , we evaluate the memory savings and end-to-end speedup of DiRotQ on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 desktop GPU ( NVIDIA Corporation, 2022 ) . For efficient 4 4 -bit INT matrix multiplication, we use the optimized kernel provided by the Nunchaku inference engine ( Li et al., 2025 ) . For the rotation operations, we implement an efficient Triton ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) kernel. Compared to the BF16 baseline, DiRotQ achieves an overall 2.1 × 2.1\times reduction in DiT inference memory, after accounting for overhead from high-precision branches, rotation matrices, and unquantized normalization layers. The memory savings mainly come from quantizing the weights of the linear layers, as activation memory accounts for only about 2 % 2\% of the weight memory. As a result, DiRotQ has nearly the same memory footprint as the INT4 weight-only quantization variant (Figure 4 a). For latency, when the batch size is 1 1 and the BF16 model fits on GPU, DiRotQ achieves a 2.3 × 2.3\times end-to-end speedup per denoising timestep compared to BF16. In contrast, the INT4 weight-only baseline provides little to no speedup, since it does not enable low-precision compute and introduces additional overhead from upcasting weights to BF16 (Figure 4 b). When increasing the batch size to 2 2 , the BF16 model no longer fits entirely in GPU memory and requires per-layer CPU offloading, while DiRotQ still fits entirely in GPU memory. This avoids offloading overhead and results in a 9.2 × 9.2\times speedup over BF16 (Figure 4 d). Figure 4 : Memory usage and one-step latency for FLUX.1-dev across batch sizes 1 and 2. While we focus on text-to-image generation, extending DiRotQ to video remains an important direction, though temporal dependencies across frames introduce additional challenges not addressed here. Qur PCA basis is also shared across timesteps to enable offline weight fusion; exploring per-timestep-group rotations under tighter memory budgets is left to future work. More broadly, although our method supports wider adoption of generative models, it does not mitigate risks of misuse such as generating harmful or misleading content. Addressing these concerns requires complementary safeguards, responsible deployment, and further research into trustworthy generative systems. 7 Conclusion In this work, we introduce DiRotQ, a rotation-aware 4-bit PTQ framework specifically designed for diffusion transformers. By leveraging PCA-based transformations to better align activation statistics, DiRotQ effectively mitigates quantization errors arising from timestep-dependent variation and activation outliers. To provide a comprehensive assessment of generative performance, we further integrate a VLM-as-a-Judge evaluation protocol, offering a holistic view of perceptual quality and prompt alignment.
